title: Dinah and the Men of Shechem

verses.text: Now Dinah, the daughter Leah had borne to Jacob, went out to visit the daughters of the land.
When Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the region, saw her, he took her and lay with her by force.
And his soul was drawn to Dinah, the daughter of Jacob. He loved the young girl and spoke to her tenderly.
So Shechem told his father Hamor, "Get me this girl as a wife."
Jacob heard that Shechem had defiled his daughter Dinah, but since his sons were with his livestock in the field, he remained silent about it until they returned.
Meanwhile, Shechem's father Hamor came to speak with Jacob.

When Jacob's sons heard what had happened, they returned from the field. They were filled with grief and fury, because Shechem had committed an outrage in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter—a thing that should not be done.
But Hamor said to them, "My son Shechem longs for your daughter. Please give her to him as his wife.
Intermarry with us; give us your daughters, and take our daughters for yourselves.
You may settle among us, and the land will be open to you. Live here, move about freely, and acquire your own property."
Then Shechem said to Dinah's father and brothers, "Grant me this favor, and I will give you whatever you ask.
Demand a high dowry and an expensive gift, and I will give you whatever you ask. Only give me the girl as my wife!"
But because Shechem had defiled their sister Dinah, Jacob's sons answered him and his father Hamor deceitfully.
"We cannot do such a thing," they said. "To give our sister to an uncircumcised man would be a disgrace to us.
We will consent to this on one condition, that you become circumcised like us—every one of your males.
Then we will give you our daughters and take your daughters for ourselves. We will dwell among you and become one people.
But if you will not agree to be circumcised, then we will take our sister and go."
Their offer seemed good to Hamor and his son Shechem.
The young man, who was the most respected of all his father's household, did not hesitate to fulfill this request, because he was delighted with Jacob's daughter.
So Hamor and his son Shechem went to the gate of their city and addressed the men of their city:
"These men are at peace with us. Let them live and trade in our land; indeed, it is large enough for them. Let us take their daughters in marriage and give our daughters to them.
But only on this condition will the men agree to dwell with us and be one people: if all our men are circumcised as they are.
Will not their livestock, their possessions, and all their animals become ours? Only let us consent to them, and they will dwell among us."
All the men who went out of the city gate listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male of the city was circumcised.
Three days later, while they were still in pain, two of Jacob's sons (Dinah's brothers Simeon and Levi) took their swords, went into the unsuspecting city, and slaughtered every male.
They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with their swords, took Dinah out of Shechem's house, and went away.
Jacob's other sons came upon the slaughter and looted the city, because their sister had been defiled.
They took their flocks and herds and donkeys, and everything else in the city or in the field.
They carried off all their possessions and women and children, and they plundered everything in their houses.

Then Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, "You have brought trouble upon me by making me a stench to the Canaanites and Perizzites, the people of this land. We are few in number; if they unite against me and attack me, I and my household will be destroyed."
But they replied, "Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?"

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Family narrative: the story of Isaac’s sons, Jacob and Esau (Genesis 25:19 to 36:43)
context.audience: Israel, named for Jacob, learning how God kept His promise through a flawed and struggling family
context.setting: Dinah, Leah’s daughter, goes out “to visit the daughters of the land” (v.1). Shechem, the son of Hamor the Hivite and prince of the region, “took her and lay with her by force” (v.2); afterward he says he loves her and asks his father to get her for him as a wife (vv.3-4). Jacob hears and says nothing until his sons come in from the fields (v.5). The brothers are “filled with grief and fury,” because Shechem “had committed an outrage in Israel” (v.7). Hamor proposes that the two peoples intermarry and share the land, and Shechem offers any bride-price they name (vv.8-12). Jacob’s sons answer “deceitfully”: they will agree if every man in the city is circumcised (vv.13-17). The men of Shechem agree, partly hoping to gain Jacob’s herds (vv.20-24). Three days later, while the men are in pain, Simeon and Levi kill every male, and the other brothers plunder the city (vv.25-29). Jacob rebukes them for making him “a stench to the Canaanites and Perizzites” (v.30), but they reply, “Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?” (v.31).
context.custom: Marriages between clans were often arranged as treaties, with land and trade rights exchanged along with brides and a bride-price. The law of Moses later required a man who violated an unbetrothed girl to marry her and pay her father, without the right ever to divorce her (Deuteronomy 22:28-29). Circumcision was the sign of God’s covenant with Abraham (17:10-14); here the brothers turn it into a weapon. Dinah herself never speaks in the chapter.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 35 brings Jacob back to Bethel, where God renews his new name Israel; Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin, and Isaac dies.
context.timelineBible: The narrator calls Shechem’s act an outrage (v.7) and does not excuse it, but neither does Jacob excuse his sons. On his deathbed he curses the anger of Simeon and Levi: “Cursed be their anger, for it is strong” (Genesis 49:7). Their tribes were later scattered, Levi among the cities of Israel as priests, and Simeon within Judah (Joshua 19:1; 21:1-3).

translation.meaning: To make unclean, to defile. A word from the language of worship used here of the violation of Dinah (also vv.13, 27).
Disgraceful folly, a shocking moral wrong. Used of sexual crimes in Israel (Deuteronomy 22:21; 2 Samuel 13:12).
Deceit. The same word Isaac used of Jacob’s trick (27:35). Jacob’s sons have learned their father’s ways.

gospelParallels.note: Do not avenge yourselves; leave room for God’s wrath.
Man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness of God.
Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them.

otBackground.note: Jacob curses the anger of Simeon and Levi.
The law on a man who violates an unbetrothed girl.
Tamar: such a thing should not be done in Israel.

overview.summary: Shechem the prince violates Dinah and then asks to marry her; her brothers pretend to agree, then Simeon and Levi massacre the city, and Jacob fears for his family’s safety.
overview.settingLine: The city of Shechem, where Jacob had bought land.
overview.placeName: Shechem, the Oak of Moreh (Tell Balata)

history.t: One of the peoples of Canaan, here ruling Shechem.
A strong city at a crossroads of the central hill country.

customs.t: Clans joined by exchanging daughters, land and trade.
Shechem offers to pay whatever they ask.

archaeology.t: Middle Bronze Age Shechem had massive walls and gates.
Not yet identified in texts outside the Bible; some link them with the Hurrians.

overview.discussion: Jacob stayed silent while others acted, and his sons answered wrong with greater wrong (vv.5, 25). How should I respond when someone I love has been badly wronged?
overview.book: The book of Genesis · 50 chapters. Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and the nations, then God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
overview.author: Moses, by tradition

historicalImage.caption: Dinah, by James Tissot (about 1896-1902, Jewish Museum, New York). Leah’s daughter “went out to visit the daughters of the land” (Genesis 34:1), and the story that follows is one of the darkest in Genesis.

currentImage.caption: Shechem (Nablus) in the pass below Mount Gerizim, in a lantern slide from about 1915. Abram’s first stop in Canaan was “the site of the Oak of Moreh at Shechem,” where he built his first altar (Genesis 12:6-7).
